Numbers & logic · 2 min read

A simple way to multiply by 11 in your head

See how the shortcut works with 34 × 11, what changes with 78 × 11, and when you need to carry a digit.

In this article
  1. Multiply by ten, then add once more
  2. The shortcut for two-digit numbers
  3. What if the middle sum is ten or more?
  4. Have a go
  5. Use the longer method when it helps
Related gameMath Rush →

Multiply by ten, then add once more

Eleven is ten plus one, so multiplying by 11 means taking ten copies of a number and adding one more.

For 34 × 11, calculate 340 + 34. The answer is 374. This method works for any number and is easy to fall back on if a shortcut slips your mind.

The shortcut for two-digit numbers

With 34, you can keep 3 and 4 on the outside and put their sum in the middle: 3, then 7, then 4. That gives 374.

To see why, line up 340 and 34 as a column addition. You have 3 hundreds, 4 + 3 tens and 4 units.

Try 52 × 11: the middle sum is 5 + 2 = 7, giving 572. Check it with 520 + 52.

What if the middle sum is ten or more?

For 78 × 11, the middle sum is 7 + 8 = 15. That means 15 tens, so you need to carry:

  1. Keep 8 in the units place.
  2. Put 5 in the tens place.
  3. Add the carried 1 to the 7 hundreds.

The answer is 858. You can check it with 780 + 78 = 858.

Have a go

Try 23 × 11, 67 × 11 and 99 × 11. The last one needs a little extra care.

Show the answers
  • 23 × 11 = 253.
  • 67 × 11 = 737.
  • 99 × 11 = 1089.

For 99, the middle sum is 18. Carrying 1 into the 9 hundreds gives 10 hundreds, so the result has four digits.

Use the longer method when it helps

For a larger number such as 126, multiplying by ten and adding the original number is still straightforward: 1260 + 126 = 1386. The two-digit shortcut needs adapting for longer numbers.

The same idea works in reverse for multiplication by 9: take ten times the number and subtract one copy. For example, 34 × 9 = 340 − 34 = 306.
